en: The *Tattvasiddhi* composed by the master Śāntarakṣita.
Homage to the glorious Vajrasattva, who removes all defilements!
Having paid homage to the Vajrayāna, the source of great bliss, I shall proclaim the *Tattvasiddhi* for the purpose of dispelling delusion. (1)
In this Vajrayāna, there are those whose mental continuums have not accumulated the latencies of wholesome roots,
who superimpose the cultivation of intrinsic existence,
and whose intellects are driven by the winds of their own conceptual constructions.
Their minds were defiled by the thick mire of the stains of the entire Kali age;
they had not yet found the means to cross the ocean of saṃsāra; and their intellects were occupied with the numerous fabrications of their own conceptual constructions.
Those fallen into the wretchedness of uneven knots and difficult passages,
their minds agitated by the force of the possession of hard-to-comprehend [doctrines],
and who have not served a teacher;
Devoid of instruction on the cultivation of the ultimate truth,
the state of the glorious Mahāsukha-Vajrasattva—

which is to be realized through other paths even in countless great aeons— is here, in this very life, effortlessly accomplished as the stable nature of all phenomena for those endowed with the methods of the Vajrayāna.
Without beginning or end,
without abode,
and pervading the mental continuums of all sentient beings.
Its nature is self-cognizable,
it is the cause of great merit,
and its characteristic is realization.

And those who do not realize the characteristics of the Mahāvajrayāna— the supreme scripture among all vehicles— which serves as the means for that [realization], for the sake of removing the cataracts of the darkness of their ignorance, something is here stated by means of both reasoning and scripture.

In this regard, it must necessarily be accepted by those possessed of discernment that objects such as form (*rūpa*), when embraced by wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*), become objects of enjoyment and bring about a distinguished result;
for it is well-established among all proponents of tenets that a distinguished causal complex (*sāmagrī*) produces only a distinguished result.
Just as the *āmalaka* fruit produced from the earth and other elements is experienced as having an astringent taste, [so too does the causal complex produce its specific result].
Furthermore, by encountering additional conditions such as the sprinkling of milk and so forth, that very same thing is perceived as sweet.

Thus, just as a cause processed by other factors is seen through direct perception itself as bringing about a specific result, so too these objects—form and the rest—produce a more distinguished result for yogins who are empowered by mantra and mudrā in the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā; this should be noted by the wise.
Since indeed nothing single is a producer, but rather the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*) is the producer, a specific effect arises precisely from a specific [additional] cause,
because the power of causes and conditions is inconceivable even for the All-Knowing Ones.
[The formal argument]: In this regard, those things which are conditioned by distinguished causes produce only a distinguished effect;
for example, myrobalan fruits and the like become sweet when treated with the sprinkling of milk.
Likewise, visible forms and other phenomena, when conditioned by distinguished causes, [produce a distinguished effect].
Thus is the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
Herein, the entity intended as the effect, whose nature is invariably concomitant with the mere production by another specific cause, is the pervading nature (*vyāpakasvabhāva*);
whereas the production by another specific cause is indeed the pervaded (*vyāpya*).
Therefore, whatever has a nature conditioned by other specific causes,
that very thing— provided there is no obstruction and no deficiency of causes— becomes a specifically distinguished effect due to the conditioning by those other specific causes,
because it is invariably concomitant with just that [conditioning].

Therefore, once the relationship of pervader (*vyāpaka*) and pervaded (*vyāpya*) has been established between those two, when the pervader is the probandum (*sādhya*), the pervaded is the logical reason (*hetu*).
For example, when the pervader such as "tree" is the probandum, the pervaded such as "śiṃśapā tree" is the reason.
Since the relationship of pervader and pervaded is already established, there is no further cause for it here beyond that very relationship of pervader and pervaded.
It should be understood in the same way here as well;
for this very reason it was said: "In all the Yoga Tantras, such as the Guhyendutilaka and others..."
There is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished by means of a mind endowed with wisdom and skillful means. ||2||
Always remaining free from doubt, one should enjoy the five objects of desire;
for through the application of medicinal powder, it is like the binding of a serpent. (3)
For one who is full of desire, eternally impassioned, devoted to song and instrumental music, and unsatiated by the pleasures of love, success is achieved; of this there is no doubt. ||4||
For one whose bodhicitta is firm and whose mind is free from attachment, no doubt should ever be entertained; for such a person, this will certainly be accomplished. ||5||
Having thoroughly examined and well-considered [the situation], the wise man should cause the entry;
otherwise, his entering the fire is not worth even a sixteenth part [of the merit].
He who, having understood reality through reality itself, cultivates resolute conviction, attains success; otherwise, he falls into the great hell. (7)
Nor can it be said that these objects, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, are causes of ruin because they are causes for the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Since afflictions are preceded by the grasping and adherence to "self" and "mine," form and the rest are not the primary cause;
for when there is a notion of self, there arises the designation of "other," and from the distinction between self and other, grasping and aversion follow.
All defects arise when these two are conjoined. ||8||
Therefore, these afflictions arise for one who possesses the view of a self;
however, for one who has attained the essence of selflessness through the internalization of selflessness,
these do not exist in that way.
If, however, sense objects were always exclusively causes of attachment, how then could they also produce a contrary cognition through aspects such as impurity?
It is by the power of habituation that these [objects] indeed produce consciousness precisely according to the superimposition [of a particular aspect].
In this way, why is it not accepted that objects function as causes for the production of specific results through specific superimpositions and specific transformations? For example:
Regarding the body of a single woman, there are three conceptualizations: "impure," "a lover," and "food"—[held respectively] by an ascetic, a lustful man, and a dog. (9)
Nor do these specific superimpositions become causes for the bondage of *saṃsāra* through such a transformation,
because of the purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala-pariśuddhi*), whereby the gift, the giver, and the recipient are not perceived as real entities.

Since the transformation of mantras and mudrās occurs through the purity of the three spheres, therefore, objects such as forms (*rūpa*) and so forth— endowed with excellence by means of mantras and the like— produce only the unsurpassed fruit.
Just as poison and the like, when consecrated by means of mantras and so forth and then consumed, produce an entirely different result such as that of an elixir (*rasāyana*),
whereas otherwise they invariably cause death for the ignorant;
in the same way, it must be thoroughly understood that sense objects, when presided over by mantras and mudrās, manifest an even more distinguished fruit.
And this has been stated in the *Śrīparamādya*: "Passion, hatred, and delusion— these three,
when they have become unbalanced, indeed turn into poison when practiced in an unbalanced manner."
Furthermore, those who have cultivated immortality through the state of immortality [attain] immortality itself. ||10||
Furthermore, it is said in the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*: "For example, Kāśyapa,
in fields of sugarcane or fields of rice, a heap of refuse becomes beneficial."
In the same way, whatever heap of defilements a bodhisattva has becomes beneficial for omniscience.

Just as poison, Kāśyapa, when held by mantras and medicinal herbs, does not cause death, even so a bodhisattva endowed with wisdom and skillful means is not cast down by the poisons of the defilements.
Furthermore, it was said by the venerable master Nāgārjuna:
"O sinless one, those afflictions, together with their roots and their limits, which consist of latent predispositions, have been abandoned."
From the onset of the afflictions until you have acquired the nectar of immortality.
Furthermore, it is said in the *Upāliparipṛcchā-sūtra*: "Passion conduces to the welfare of sentient beings for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, because of his affection for sentient beings."

Because one observes a difference in effects due to a difference in causal conditions, and because of the realization of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), no form of attachment whatsoever can possibly arise toward that [object].
However, for the attainment of the fruit of unsurpassed great bliss (*anuttaramahāsukha*), there is no other means than this.
By those very pleasures—such as food, recreation, and so forth—that fruit is brought to manifestation; he for whom prosperity acts as a precursor would be of such a kind.
How could one who has arisen from a different nature become such?
Therefore, it is said in the *Samvara-tantra*:
The self indeed is all-buddhahood and all-heroism;
therefore, through union with one's own presiding deity, one should accomplish the self alone. (12)
Yoga does not arise with respect to reflected images or cast [images] and the like;
therefore, for the yogin, the deities arise from the great exertion of the bodhicitta. ||13||
One should not afflict oneself with ascetic practices by abandoning one's own self;
rather, happiness should be maintained at ease, for this one is a perfectly awakened Buddha who has not yet come. (14)

Success is not attained through excessive purity, nor by restrictive observances, nor by austerities, nor by difficult penances; it is achieved neither by ascetic practices nor by rules, but through happiness and joy. (15)

Just as the Blessed One has stated that form and so forth—which arise from those [elements] and transform into pleasure—are causes for the unsurpassed fruit, so too are the transformations of pleasure arising from contact.
If it is argued that this is not the case because it contradicts scripture, the scripture states: "From the cultivation of the pleasure of specific types of contact, one brings about its fruit."
If it is argued that there is a contradiction because that [practice] has been prohibited, we say no;
for the prohibition concerns a restricted scope.

For those who are devoid of wisdom and skillful means, who—through their attachment to the grasping of "self" and "mine"—are ignorant of the dedication [of merit], indulge in specific types of sensory contact, [it is indeed prohibited].
For those whose bodies are gripped by ignorance, sense objects become the cause of their downfall.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One:
"Those who abide in the state of a monk, and those men who are devoted to speculative reasoning..."
And one should not teach the reality to those who abide in old age. ||16||
The Blessed One, having taken them into consideration, spoke this prohibition.
And it was said in the *Śrī-samāja*:
"Those devoid of gnosis assert the ten paths of wholesome action. (17)
Likewise, it is also said in the *Vairocanābhisambodhi*:
"Knowledge or even the training, when taught without skillful means,"
Indeed, for the sake of the Śrāvakas among them, the Great Hero [taught] thus for their deliverance. ||18||

But for those whose forms are embraced by wisdom and skillful means, who seek the distinguished fruit, and who experience the fruit of distinguished dedication because they have realized the reality of the ultimate nature of phenomena— not even in the slightest do they share in that fault; rather, being endowed with a distinguished intellect, they become possessors of unsurpassed contentment due to the purity of their minds.
Therefore, this distinction between merit and non-merit is established solely by way of a particular intention (*āśaya*),
and not as an objective form existing according to the actual state of things.
And it was said by Āryadeva:
Whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, everything that arises from the volition of Bodhisattvas becomes entirely auspicious, because their minds are under their own control. (19)

Therefore, regarding the merits and demerits produced by intention (*saṅkalpa*), for one who possesses a particularly distinguished intention formed by other causes with respect to forms and so forth, a corresponding distinguished fruit must necessarily be admitted for him— even by others who are unwilling— on account of that particular disposition (*āśaya*).
For this very reason, it was said by the Blessed One:
"Phenomena are like an illusion;
for one who has resolute conviction, all enjoyments are appropriate.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The gift of faith from a monk who possesses pride is not to be consumed.
Furthermore, it is said in the *Saṃvaratantra*:
"Everything has the characteristic of space, and space itself is without characteristics."
And indeed, the entire triple world without exception is like an illusion. ||20||
Just as an illusion is seen and touched from every side, yet is not apprehended at all, so too is the existence of the entire world;
by means of this seal, the yogi should purify the three worlds. (21)
Furthermore, it is said in the *Sarvadevasamāgama-tantra*: "By those very things by which fools are bound, the Buddhas sport here;
all [this] is through the complete yoga, otherwise they go out like a lamp. (22)
And it is further said:
"They practice the secret supramundane conduct without conceptualization;
otherwise, negligence would arise, for conceptualization is applicable therein. (23)

By means of a non-conceptual state, in every form and at all times, having taken recourse in the state of being (*sattva*) free from doubt, one then attains accomplishment without a shadow of a doubt. ||24||
One who possesses such courage will never incur bondage, regardless of their state at all times,
nor even when engaged in any form of conduct whatsoever.
One whose movement through all conduct is performed with a non-conceptual mind is indeed not bound by the enjoyment of any of the sense faculties. //26//
And it is further said:
"For those who perceive all this as empty in form with an eye that is itself empty, and who are free from conceptual construction, fearlessness shall arise. (27)
Furthermore, in that very same [text]:
"By meditating on all things as having the nature of space with a mind that has the nature of space, non-conceptuality and fearlessness arise. (28)
And it is further said: "What is the vow of yogins?
One should then perform all actions with skillful means and without hesitation;
through such a state of being free from doubt, one attains the most excellent of all vows. (29)
What is called austerity (tapas)?
One should always perform all actions with a state of mind free from conceptual construction and devoid of doubt; this is the highest of all austerities. (30)
For one who indulges in sense objects with a non-conceptual mind, that austerity—whether performed with contempt or not—is difficult to overcome. (31)
But he who would apply all actions through wisdom, uniting them all in the state of emptiness—this indeed is the austerity of the great-souled ones. (32)
The practice of those great-souled ones consists of the movement of conduct free from doubt, by means of a non-conceptual mind in the form of the transference of wisdom. //33//
If the mind should transfer elsewhere without wisdom and means,
it is certainly taught that this [state] bestows great enlightenment. ||34||
For those yogins who are diligent and follow the path of non-conceptualization,
he has created all beings for their enjoyment.
For those whose minds are non-conceptual by nature, mindfulness arises from wisdom; it is refined, takes on the form of that [object], and is reflected upon the mirror of wisdom. (36)
He who perceives [the world] as being like a reflection in a mirror, a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a magical trick— he is known as a Lord.
Like lightning, a city of the Gandharvas, and the ripening of karma, they perceive the conditioned world as having that very form; thus are all living beings said to be dependent upon it. (38)
Thus it has been said.
Therefore, there is no abiding state for anything wherein attachment could occur.

And when, even by means of such phenomena that are like an illusion, through the transformation resulting from the touch of pleasure born of a particular enjoyment, not even the slightest distinguished fruit is attained—
In that case, why is it not accepted?
[For] these are not stable by way of their own nature,
but rather are characterized solely by appearance.

If these [mental factors], through the power of the practice of distinguished cultivation (*viśiṣṭabhāvanā*), attain the status of being causes for the attainment of the noble, unsurpassed fruit (*āryānuttaraphala*) in relation to their effects such as distinguished pleasure and mental well-being (*saumanasya*), then there is no fault whatsoever.
Thus it has been said in the *Śrīparamādya*:
The self indeed is all-buddhahood and all-heroism;
therefore, through union with one's own presiding deity, one should accomplish the self alone. (39)
Through difficult and intense observances, the body withers and becomes distressed;
from distress the mind is distracted, and through distraction, success is otherwise [than desired]. (40)
And through the firmness of the mental form, all happiness becomes stable;
through sufferings, it becomes unsteady or even reaches cessation. ||41||
Furthermore, it is said in the *Laukikalokottaravajratantra*:
"Accomplishment is attained through bliss; accomplishment is not achieved by tormenting the body.
For Buddhahood arises from meditative absorption (*samādhi*) through all forms of happiness. (42)
Through intense fasting and other such practices, as well as through thirst and other afflictions, the body is tormented;
from this bodily torment comes distraction, and from distraction, there is no accomplishment.
Those of inferior resolve do not achieve success; therefore, these are proclaimed to be "difficult practices. (43)
Furthermore, it is said in the *Śrīsamāja-tantra*:
"One who practices with difficult observances and arduous hardships does not attain accomplishment;
but by enjoying all objects of desire, one attains accomplishment swiftly. (44)
One who subsists on alms should not recite [the mantra], nor should he take no pleasure in begging;
rather, he should recite the mantra with his limbs unimpaired, even while enjoying all objects of desire. 45.
Having attained stability of body, speech, and mind, one attains enlightenment;
otherwise, one certainly undergoes untimely death and is cooked in hell. ||46||

Therefore, when the mind— which is by nature luminous like a crystal stone— is endowed with specific mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by forms and other objects, characterized by pleasure and mental well-being, that [luminosity] would reach a state of ultimate excellence therein through the power of specific practice, being embraced by wisdom and skillful means;
just as, for example, wisdom, arts, crafts, and so forth [reach excellence].

The knowledge of the yogin arises from a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of objects such as sound; through the power of repeated practice of meditation, it emerges at the culmination of the intensity of cultivation as a state of meditative absorption (*samāhita*), characterized by a supreme and eternal nature—
just as [it is established] for the Sugata and others in their own system.

And in the world, just as [states such as] desire, grief, fear, and madness are observed, so too are pleasure, mental ease, and the like produced by touch and other [sensations]; therefore, these too possess ultimate particularity (paramaviśeṣa). This is the perception of a contradictory nature (svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi).
Here too, there is an effect characterized by pleasure, mental ease, and so forth, which is the opposite of suffering and the like;
and when that [effect] is perceived as attaining the state of being naturalized through the power of practice,
it then causes the cessation of its opposite— suffering, mental unease, and so forth.
And it presents its own array of qualities (*guṇavyūha*).
Thus, by being established here as a totality of cultivation (*sāmagrī-bhāvanatā*), it excludes any opportunity for that which is its opposite, such as suffering and so forth.
For example, heat and the like, when perceived as contrary to cold and the like, establish the absence of cold and so forth.
Just as things that are mutually contradictory are not perceived in a single location,
so too it is impossible for these two— pleasure and pain— to exist in any way within a single continuum (santāna), because that [continuum] is itself contradictory [to their coexistence].

Therefore, when one has fully internalized pleasure, mental joy, and so forth, one can by no means attribute even the possibility of suffering and the like [to oneself]; thus it is rightly said that "the perception of what is contradictory to the nature [of something] establishes the absence of that form.
When reaching the ultimate limit of excellence, specific practice is the cause, as in the case of wisdom, craftsmanship, the arts, and so on.
This should be understood as being due to the perception of something incompatible with those specific qualities.
Furthermore, if the cessation of even those specific qualities that are being cultivated is desired, [then...]

In that case, even the "earth-totality" (*pṛthvī-kṛtsna*) and so forth would likewise bring about cessation for those who have reached the culmination of meditative cultivation; yet this is not accepted. For those things which, by virtue of reaching the culmination of cultivation, have attained their own essential nature, do not undergo recurrence—just as the earth-totality and the like do not.

Having attained their own existence and being dependent upon their respective specific qualities, pleasure, mental ease, and so forth do not cease; for in the case of their cessation, there would be no cause.
However, as for those factors such as defects (*doṣa*) which partake in cessation, at that time their existence does not occur;
consequently, even the arising of suffering would not take place,
for that is impossible upon reaching the ultimate limit of excellence.
Otherwise, it would follow that even after liberation there would still be saṃsāra; this is neither accepted nor logically tenable.

Even those who do not accept the arising of saṃsāra for one who has attained liberation must admit that at that time [saṃsāra] ceases due to the absence of its cause, namely, the latent impressions of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*).

That arising which occurs for the sake of others is not of the nature of saṃsāra, because it proceeds there through the power of the influence of former vows, and not through the power of latent predispositions (vāsanā).
Therefore, just as cyclic existence does not arise immediately after liberation,
so too suffering does not arise for the mind immediately after reaching the ultimate limit of the excellence of happiness; because it is pure by nature, that very mind is like a multi-colored gem.
Then, by whatever [state] one is perfumed, in each case it manifests a more distinguished nature characterized by the quality of non-reversion, through the power of habituation.
For this very reason it has been said:
"By whichever state the minds of men are conjoined..."
By that, he attains identity with it, just as a gem assumes the form of everything around it. ||47||
Therefore, when all of this is dedicated by means of a distinguished dedication, it becomes a bringer of distinguished fruit.
Consequently, there is no such thing as a "dedication that is not dedicated.
And by the power of the impetus of prior karma, it comes to be exactly so.
Otherwise, the specific dedication would be futile, and it would be unreliable in all cases.
Thus it is said in the *Jinajananī*:
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives divine ointments to the Tathāgatas or to the shrines of the Tathāgatas.
It occurs to him thus:"
"By this root of merit, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
may divine, exquisite sensations of touch be manifested for all sentient beings in those Buddha-fields. Thus should be the dedication.
Furthermore, Subhūti, it occurs to a bodhisattva mahāsattva:

"By the mere power of my mental aspiration and resolve, may I present the five desirable sense-qualities to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to the communities of their disciples, and to all sentient beings.

As he perceives this, it occurs to him: "By this root of goodness, when I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in my own buddha-field, [may there be] for the community of disciples and for the sentient beings..."
And by the mere power of their mental aspiration and resolve, let the desired qualities of sensual pleasure manifest.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
bodhisattva mahāsattvas give the gift of the five qualities of sensual pleasure to all sentient beings together with the perfectly enlightened Buddhas, and so forth.
Furthermore, by the very power of the impulse of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it functions in this way toward observed effects.

Just as in the world a fruit such as the *mātuluṅga* takes on the aforementioned form through the application of lac-dye and so forth, so too, for this consciousness (*citta*), through the cultivation of external touch and other sensations, that very pleasure and so forth— having acquired a specific quality through the penetration of particular mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)— again becomes directed toward that very same object.
Because the mind is attached to that [object], it becomes colored by it and becomes firmly established therein.

Just as in the case of the dhatura, cotton-seed, pomegranate, and so forth, where a specific quality is induced by other causes, the fruit is perceived in that very same way because of the capacity that has been infused.
In the same way, the mind also—producing specific states such as pleasure and mental joy born from contact and so forth—becomes the bringer of increasingly superior fruits.
Because it is not non-attached to its antidotes, there is no arising of those antidotes; for it is turned away from them and because it is characterized by happiness.
Thus, it is demonstrated in the *Śrīparamādya*:
"O King, no opportunity for all-pervasive suffering, dejection, and the like should be granted. ||47||
Furthermore, it is said in the *Sarvadevasamāgama-tantra*: "Among gods, asuras, and spirits, there is no awakening;
by reciting [this], they experience bliss throughout their entire bodies. (48)
Therefore, they go beyond to nirvana like lamps;
the fire of nirvana is most terrible, for it leaves not even ashes behind. //49//
Therein reality does not exist; there are no sense objects, nor the elements;
there is neither mind nor mental factors, nor ego, nor even intellect. (50)
There is no sentient being, no wisdom, no mind, and indeed nothing at all;
it has the form of one established in deep sleep, free from conceptual construction, and devoid of self. //51//
There is neither perception nor activity, neither form nor quality anywhere;
that is designated as Nirvana, and liberation is indeed partless. || 52 ||
Having realized that the nature of the state of cyclic existence is the absence of intrinsic nature, one should then be known as awakened, even if one does not desire nirvāṇa. //53//

Having understood the true nature of reality and its conformity [to that], as well as the fact that the intrinsic nature of things is the absence of intrinsic nature, the heroic one who would attain nirvāṇa does so without [external] accomplishment. //54//
Furthermore, for one of inferior mind, there arises the loss of what has been accomplished, in that having attained supreme enlightenment, he falls away before reaching final perfection. //55//
What evil has not been committed by that thief who steals his own self—he who would not fulfill with happiness the attainment of this body, which is the very nature of the Buddha? (56)
He possesses neither vigor nor is he established in courage, who, having attained supreme enlightenment, proceeds toward nirvāṇa without having accomplished his task. //57//
There is no one more base than he, nor any person more wicked, who, having attained supreme enlightenment, abandons his own body. (58)
That vigor which, having been awakened among all forms of vigor, proceeds forth—one who is thus engaged is not bound, even while delighting in the enjoyment of all the sense faculties. (59)
Furthermore, it is said in the *Vimuktisamudyātana-tantra*:
"Since there is no vow of reality for men that bestows such great fruit, how can the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those whose conviction is fixed on the mind ever be abandoned? (60)
The mind of one established in the vows of Yoga Tantra is not purified by that [mere view];
solely due to having a divergent view, even one who is awakened perishes. //61//
Other men who have attained awakening do not experience the fruit of ingratitude;
like a lamp, they proceed toward nirvāṇa and do not enjoy worldly success. ||62||
No one devoid of being (sattva) is born from his own body;
and he who attains nirvāṇa is one whose desires are directly perceived. ||63||
Those men who have attained nirvāṇa here through the cause of awakening have then abandoned infinite pleasures and achieved their desired fruit. ||64||
And it is further said:
"Just as mercury, through contact with fire, assumes its true nature;
it is neither burned nor seen, nor does it go forth as mere smoke. (65)
Just as [cow dung] is gathered again by means of the application of holding it together with cow dung, one should understand that knowledge is exactly like that, equal to the Mahāmudrā. 66.
And the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: whatever things have reached the ultimate limit of excellence do not regress, such as liberation and so forth.
Pleasure, mental ease, and the like are of the nature of causes that have reached the ultimate limit of excellence.
This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

And the other [reason] is as follows: for those things which are cultivated become, through the power of the practice of cultivation, situated at the ultimate limit of the highest degree of meditative concentration (*samāhita*), just like wisdom, arts, crafts, and so forth.
And blisses and mental joys, embraced by wisdom and skillful means and produced from a specific kind of contact, are cultivated;
therefore, they too reach the highest excellence.
This is precisely a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Therefore, in this case as well, the process of internalizing [the practice] is necessarily concomitant with reaching the very limit of excellence; and by the power of a specific kind of cultivation, that [internalization] attains a state characterized by non-recurrence.
Once it has attained that intrinsic nature, it can no longer be turned back by anything else whatsoever.
For example, the specific changes produced by fire in wood and the like do not cease to belong to that [wood],
because its characteristic of being burnt and so forth possesses the property of non-recurrence.
For this very reason it has been said:
Furthermore, burning never produces any transformation whatsoever in [certain things], whereas from the opposite [cause], some transformation does arise, as in the case of wood and gold. (67)

In the case of gold and the like, a specific quality produced by fire arises when its previous continuum is interrupted; this is brought about through a contrary cause, resulting in the manifestation of a different nature, just as in the case of fire, water, and so forth.
Even in the case of all that has been melted gold, another distinct quality characterized by a solid nature is produced, and a different quality permeated by its own nature comes into being.
In this context, there is a specific state of joy arising in the mind from the enjoyment of sensory objects.
As that very cause is cultivated further and further, reaching its ultimate consummation, there is no turning back,
because the intellect is partial toward it;
for the intellect, being attached to that and having acquired its qualities, takes up that very cause.
And in the opposite case, because of its primary nature, it does not turn back in any way whatsoever.
And as follows: wherever there is reaching the limit of excellence, there there is the state of being assimilated (sātmībhāva).
For example—[in the case of] a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) regarding his birth, nature, and so forth:
through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there arises cruelty.

For instance, in the case of a certain Vedic scholar who observes the great vows (*mahāvrata*), by making cruelty habitual through cultivation, he attains identity with it; and that [cruelty], like self-awareness, pleasure, mental ease, and so forth, exists throughout the entire continuum [of consciousness].
Self-cognizing direct perception is established; that too exists there with an uninterrupted flow due to the power of the yoga of meditative cultivation.
Because there is an absence of causes for the interruption of the flow, causes for the interruption of the flow of suffering and so forth are not found.
For indeed, no discerning person, having understood suffering and the like as being of a beneficial nature, would abandon them,
nor would they seek out the causes for their arising again.
A discerning person would not be otherwise at any point; anyone other than that would be like one intoxicated and so forth.
Therefore, let alone the attainment of the ultimate limit of excellence, [the mere initial effort is sufficient].
However, even by practicing [the opposite] for only a very short time, because the intellect is bound to that which is beneficial to it, no cause contrary to that can ever arise here.
Indeed, no one who knows would intentionally take up a snake, poison, thorns, and so forth.
For by the power of a specific habituation, that [contrary cause] becomes assimilated and brings about its own result.
And since those [causes] have already been rejected by the intellect as being of the nature of what is to be abandoned, there is a severance of their continuity.
A reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) establishes that very nature.
Nor is the reason unestablished;
for even through a specific cultivation, excellence is attained in wisdom and the like, and thus practice certainly exists.
Therefore, there is neither the fault of being unestablished nor that of being inconclusive.
That by which happiness, mental pleasure, and so forth, being practiced, do not operate toward their opposite, such as suffering and so forth, is not contradictory;
for it does not establish suffering, which is the opposite of what is to be proven.
This is because the subjects of the examples (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) are also well-established for all disputants;
by means of these [examples], it is observed that wisdom, arts, crafts, and so forth, attain specific distinctions through individual human practice.
Furthermore, as it has been said: "The meditations on the foul (*aśubha*) are the antidotes to attachment."
Loving-kindness is the antidote to hatred;
dependent origination is the antidote to delusion.
In that regard, from passion comes detachment and cessation.
If it is argued that this is because they are contradictory [to passion], we say no;
for if that were the case, then even while one is becoming habituated to passion, detachment would arise simultaneously.
Therefore, it is said in the Root Tantra:
"Aho! Indeed, the knowledge of passion of all Buddhas is unstained;
having destroyed both passion and dispassion, they proclaim all-bliss. (68)
Furthermore, desire and the other afflictions do not constitute natural transgressions;
otherwise, the stream-enterer would not attain the path, since he continues to function without having abandoned desire and the rest.
Furthermore, it was stated by the Blessed One in the *Śīlapaṭala*: "A bodhisattva may even violate the ten wholesome actions for the sake of others.
For example, if a certain woman seeking sensual pleasure were to give up her life on account of a bodhisattva, one must sustain her life by indulging in her desire and so forth."
In the same way, seeing one who has committed great evil, he deprives him of life,
yet that person does not go to a state of woe;
rather, [the savior] produces a much greater amount of merit.

If these [afflictions], such as attachment and the rest, were inherently reprehensible (*prakṛtisāvadya*), then how could they not be causes for miserable rebirths? And how could they be described as causes for abundant jewels and merit? Therefore, they do not possess inherent reprehensibility.
However, they bring about specific qualities due to the particularity of the individual's mental continuum (*pudgala-santāna*).

For example, a *ketakī* flower that has been consumed by a scent-elephant (*gandhahastin*) transforms into musk and the like, whereas when consumed by other elephants, it causes them to become unbearable.
Therefore, in that case, there is no fault regarding the *ketakī* flower;
likewise, even passion and the other afflictions, when occurring within a purified continuum, produce a specifically distinguished result.
This is due to the connection with a particular intention (*āśaya*).
For example, milk, when consumed by snakes and the like, is transformed into the nature of poison,
whereas when consumed by other humans, it attains the state of nectar (*amṛta*).
Thus, even these [afflictions] such as passion and the like become bringers of distinguished results when they reside in one who possesses a particular disposition;
it is not because their nature is inherently faultless.

The formal argument (*hetu-prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever possesses a distinguished continuum brings about a distinguished fruit, just like *ketakī* flowers and the like; and passion (*rāga*) and other such states reside within a distinguished continuum. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*).

In this case as well, the mere transformation resulting from the application within a specific continuum produces a capacity that is unimpeded and brings about a specific fruit, just like the causal complex of the final moment;
for such is its very nature.
He indeed performs that which arises from the connection with those very [causes], because an obstruction is impossible;
and if an obstruction were possible, there would be no cognition.

Therefore, in this case as well, because it arises from a specific transformation (*pariṇāma*), it does not depend on anything else; thus, it is said to be "invariably concomitant" (*tanmātrānubandha*) with that [transformation] alone.
Furthermore, there is no obstruction to the absence of delay (*kṣepābhāva*) therein, nor is there an absence of delay at the end of the absence of delay in something other than the absence of delay.
Because of the impossibility of that which is to be observed;
thus, by means of the certainty of the necessary connection with that alone, the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) has been stated.
Likewise, the alchemist—

Likewise, due to the penetration by the mercury of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), it attains a state of mastery and produces a different form that is indeed distinguished from its previous nature. Similarly, through the power of the penetration by mercury such as mercury-essence (*pārada*) stabilized within copper and other metals, it produces an entirely different state;
moreover, it becomes free from defects and acquires the quality of non-recurrence—this should be understood here as well.
Otherwise, mercury and other substances would not possess the power to transform copper and the like.
Thus, from the observation of such efficacy, their existence is understood most clearly;
otherwise, there would be no efficacy whatsoever.
And so it has been said:
"Having taken this image of impurity, one fashions from it an image of the jewel-like Victor, which is priceless;
therefore, take up with great firmness that which is most piercing to the mind, known as the thought of enlightenment (bodhicitta). (69)
Furthermore, with merit the body is happy and with wisdom the mind is happy;
remaining in saṃsāra for the sake of others, by what means could the compassionate one be distressed? (70)
Furthermore, just as a certain wealthy man who practices alchemy, having acquired the greatness of those qualities through the combination of specific medicinal herbs,
possesses the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) and other qualities that endure as long as *saṃsāra* lasts; so it is here.

In the very same way, why would one not desire the welfare of sentient beings—one who has produced the elixir born from the enjoyment of sublime objects, who has established his natural vows throughout the cycle of existence, who is devoted to the welfare of others, whose entire multitude of qualities is concentrated in meditative absorption, and who has realized the essence of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta)? Furthermore:
"One does not attain supreme awakening, which is free from afflictions, without having reached the ultimate state."
One whose afflictions have arisen is unable to accomplish even what is beneficial for oneself;
thus, by you who have applied firm vigor for the attainment of awakening, the afflictions were not utterly consumed, but were reduced to the insignificance of a mere blade of grass. (71)
Seized by the knowledge of mindfulness, the afflictions—lightened by the accomplishment of various virtues—have become nothing but instruments for your awakening.
By this very means, your intellect thereafter did not take as its object that which is delusive; thus, even the streams of birth in this world were made into a field for virtues. (72)
Furthermore, is that omniscient knowledge— which exists at the culmination of the excellence of cultivation— conceptual (*savikalpaka*) or non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*)?
In this regard, if it is maintained that it is exclusively non-conceptual, [then...]
In that case, how can that which has arisen through the power of conceptualization in meditation be non-conceptual?
For it is in no way possible for a non-conceptual cognition to be produced from a conceptual consciousness.
If, on the other hand, non-conceptuality consists in the cessation of the latencies of the primary and secondary afflictions, [then...]
That is incorrect,
because once the latencies of the primary and secondary afflictions have ceased, what else could remain that would be conceptual?
For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for anything other than those [latencies].
Nor is there any established proof that is authoritative;
for those entities are not perceptible, because perception arises from the capacity of the sense faculty, light, mental attention, and the object.
There is no cognition that establishes [the object] while being devoid of the form of the apprehender,
because its nature is the opposite of that [object].
Nor is there inference.
For that [inference] as well is preceded by the apprehension of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*).

Without a cognition devoid of the dual forms of the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*), neither the future mark called "effect" (*kārya*) nor the mark called "essential nature" (*svabhāva*) is perceived.
Nor could there be a comprehension of it based on non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
Because that [reason] is the object of negation;
therein, first of all, the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*),
since the relationship of cause and effect is untenable.
For an effect does not arise from a cause that has perished,
because that which is non-existent lacks the capacity to produce;
nor does it arise from one that has not perished.
Because when examining the time of the engagement of an activity in that which has already arisen, the consequence of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) would follow;
for how could that which is devoid of activity possess the status of a producer, being like a sky-flower?
Therefore it has been said:
The arising of a sprout does not occur from a seed that has perished, nor from one that has not perished;
indeed, you state that all arising is like the arising of an illusion. (73)

O Protector, that which was taught by you regarding arising, cessation, and so forth, as well as sentient beings, life-principles, and the like—that was spoken by you as being of interpretable meaning; it is indeed conventional reality. (74)
Therefore, since the relationship between producer and produced is logically untenable in reality, there is no "effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*) here due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Nor is a "nature-reason" (*svabhāvahetu*) possible in any way, because its nature would be entirely beyond perception.
Because the connection with those [objects] alone is not established;
and since non-perception (*anupalambha*) also serves as a means of negation, there is no occasion here [for such a claim].

Furthermore, since no other reason (*hetu*) or separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is accepted, how can the certainty of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) be asserted? Thus it has been said:
An entity is not born from itself, nor from another, nor from both;
it is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent. At that time, how and of what could there be an arising? (75)
Therefore, from that ultimate perspective, that cognition is untenable;
how could it be non-conceptual?
For it is not admitted that things such as a sky-lotus possess either conceptual or non-conceptual status.
Nor does this reflection arise regarding it, because it serves no purpose for human aims, like a lotus in the sky;
and even if it were admitted, there would be no purpose whatsoever in doing so.

Because that [object] lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), nothing to be established by it is tenable; nor is that which does not perform the function of establishing anything designated as a "means of proof" (*sādhana*) therein.

Therefore, we maintain that all cognition whatsoever, being dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*) and existing in the form of the aspects of the apprehended and the apprehender, is conceptual (*savikalpaka*).
By this, consciousness—which possesses the forms of the grasped and the grasper within the three realms—is designated as "the conceptualization of conditions.
Therefore, it is said in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:
"The noble one perceives neither delusion nor reality in between them."
Error itself would be the reality, because reality exists within it.
For if a sign were to arise even after all delusion has been shaken off, that itself would be his delusion, like an impure cataract. (77)

In that regard, when there is the exclusion of the superimposition of contrary objects, a specific result manifests through reaching the culmination of the intensification of the cultivation of that specific object;
this is because pleasure and so forth possess a single nature— the nature of the absence of both internal and external intrinsic natures—
due to their dependence on the particularity of the practice of cultivation.

Like the cognition of that very form, it proceeds as a stream of the same kind, endowed with the distinction between the cognized object and the cognizing subject, possessing a determined nature, an uninterrupted continuity, and specific qualities; having attained mastery over its own mind, even though it is conceptual, it discerns all objects exactly as they exist.
Because his form is embraced by wisdom and skillful means, it is said for this very reason in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:
"My vehicle is not the Mahāyāna; it is neither sound nor syllables."
Nor indeed is meditative absorption or liberation without the sphere of non-appearance. //78//
But the Mahāyāna is the vehicle for those who have mastery over meditative concentration.
The body is mind-made, adorned with the flowers of divine mastery. ||79||

Thus, everything has been explained by demonstrating the specific nature of the effect based on the specific nature of the cause. Furthermore, the conceptualization of name, genus, and so forth, is superimposed.

Even determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), which follows the presence and absence of the object, is said to have an indistinct appearance (*aspaṣṭābha*) by the venerable teacher Dharmakīrti himself in his *Laukikapramāṇaparīkṣā*.

Where the appearance of the grasped and the grasper is perceived as distinct, there knowledge, though appearing unclear, appears as if it were clear. For example, knowledge free from conceptual constructions such as name, genus, and so forth, becomes clear in its appearance.
Cognition is differentiated by the distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and the cognition itself; therefore,
the Teacher also demonstrated its lack of clarity by relying on the conceptualization of name, genus, and so forth,
and not by relying on the distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and the cognition itself.
Therefore, for that [cognition] which has acquired a specific quality through the experience of the form of the object, there is an absence of a determination of something heterogeneous to it.
For that vivid appearance which has attained the state of being naturalized, there is no sublater,
and there is indeed a prover.

That which is characterized by the attainment of its becoming one's own nature was explained previously, like [the states of] desire, grief, fear, madness, and so forth. Now, if it is claimed that the knowledge appearing in the form of the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and self-awareness reaches the ultimate limit of excellence for the sake of knowing everything—
that is not the case.
Because it is established by the web of conceptual construction (*kalpanājāla*).
In that case, how can even that pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), which is devoid of all forms, possess the capacity to delimit all objects of knowledge?
For a cognition that is without appearance (*nirābhāsa*) cannot, in any way, possess the quality of being a delimiter.
And this is contradicted by reasoning:

since it is impossible for a single entity devoid of parts to possess a threefold nature, self-awareness is held to be the fruit through the distinction between the object known and the knowing subject. (80)
Now, if it is argued that this is simply its inherent nature— that upon reaching the limit of its excellence, it becomes the cognition of everything—
then that inherent nature is equally present in our position as well. For instance,

although consciousness appears differentiated by the distinction between the apprehended object and the apprehending subject, upon reaching the limit of its excellence, that very same specific form arises.
If one perceives the entire range of objects exactly as they truly exist,
has that capacity of theirs been devoured by a crow? Furthermore,
since it is devoid of the whole multitude of conceptual constructions, one must abide in some state [of realization] that such is the case.

Conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), however, is established by means of perception and other valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) as existing within the mental continua (*santāna*) of all sentient beings;
and through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), when one attains the state of identification (*sātmībhāva-samāpatti*), one understands everything.
For example, whatever [is perceived], that very thing...

Thus, whatever is cultivated, upon reaching the culmination of the intensity of that cultivation, brings about its own naturalization—just as, for example, [a person] brings about aversion toward the birth-status of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*).
And since the entire threefold world is cultivated as being for one's enjoyment, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Saṃvara Tantra*:
For the Blessed One, Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata, is indeed all yogas;
the entire threefold world without exception is his object of enjoyment. (81)
Furthermore, it is said in the *Sarvadevasamāgama-tantra*:
"Whatever fourfold elements exist, and whatever else is found within the world—all these are declared to be the requisites for yogins whose minds have attained accomplishment. (82)
Having attained the Mahāmudrā and proclaiming it as the Great Being, I shall cultivate everything word by word through the yoga of reality. 83.

Thus, and so forth—the becoming one's own nature (*sātmībhāva*) of that which is bound only by reaching the ultimate limit of the intensity of cultivation occurs wherever it may be; in each such place, it brings about that state of being one's own nature.
All objects existing within the three worlds are constantly cultivated as being the means for achieving happiness, mental well-being, and so forth.
Therefore, it is said in the *Saṃvara-tantra*:
"Whatever sense faculty comes under the range [of consciousness], by its very nature, through the yoga of non-meditative equipoise, all shall become composed of the Buddha. (84)
Furthermore, it is said in the *Sarvakalpasamuccaya-tantra*:
"In brief, the five Buddhas are known as the five strands of sensual pleasure. (85)
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Śrī Guhyasamāja Tantra*:
"One should visualize the deities through entities such as form, sound, and so forth. (86)
Therefore, when they too reach the culmination of the excellence of that cultivation, they attain the state of being identical with it; thus, they come within the range of its perception.
Consequently, even conceptual cognition, when produced by the power of cultivation, partakes in a specific nature and becomes the abode of all virtues.
For that indeed is the fruit of all accomplishments, the cause of all worlds and so forth;
it is the cause for remaining until the end of saṃsāra and the performer of the welfare of all sentient beings. ||88||
That must be understood with effort; I am to be eradicated through effort.
When that is known, everything designated as "reality" (tattva) becomes fully understood. ||89||
Thus ends the treatise named *Śrītattvasiddhi*, the *Prāvṛtatantra*. One should practice [it]. ||86||

Therefore, when they too reach the ultimate limit of the intensification of that cultivation, they attain the state of being identical with it; thus, they also come within the range of its objective domain.
Consequently, [it is] conceptual.
